title: CompTIA SecAI+
realWorldValue: The CY0-001 is CompTIA's first dedicated AI security credential, validating practitioner skills to secure AI systems, leverage AI to enhance security posture and automate tasks, and apply AI governance, risk, and compliance at scale. It targets security professionals with several years of experience moving into AI-focused roles such as AI security architect, MLOps security engineer, and AI governance specialist as organisations deploy generative AI and agentic systems.

skills: 1.1: Compare and contrast various AI types and techniques used in cybersecurity.
questions.question:
A security operations team is building a model to detect previously unseen malware variants based on a labelled corpus of millions of known-good and known-bad portable executable files. Each sample is tagged with its verdict, and analysts want the model to predict the verdict for new files. The team must select a training approach that uses the labels they already have.

Which training technique fits this requirement?

choices.text: Supervised learning, because the model is trained against labelled input-output pairs to predict a known target variable.
choices.explanation: Supervised learning is defined by training on labelled examples where the ground-truth class is known.

choices.text: Unsupervised learning, because clustering the binaries will surface the malware families without needing labels.
choices.explanation: Unsupervised learning discards available labels, which wastes the analyst-verified ground truth the team already has.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning, because the model can be rewarded each time it correctly flags a malicious binary at inference time.
choices.explanation: Reinforcement learning relies on an environment and reward signal at runtime, not a static labelled corpus.

choices.text: Federated learning, because the labelled samples can be distributed across endpoints without centralising the training data.
choices.explanation: Federated learning describes where training happens, not how labels are used; it does not by itself imply label-based classification.

questions.tip: Identify which learning paradigm explicitly consumes labelled ground truth during training.
questions.explanation:
When the dataset includes verified labels and the goal is to predict that label on new samples, the standard paradigm is supervised learning.

**Why it works:** The model minimises error against known correct outputs, learning a mapping from features to the labelled class.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Unsupervised learning: Ignores the existing labels and groups data without a verdict target.
- Reinforcement learning: Needs a reward-emitting environment, not a static dataset.
- Federated learning: Refers to distribution of training, not whether labels are used.

questions.question:
During an internal review of a phishing-detection pipeline, an architect notes that the model must understand the semantic meaning of email body text, including sarcasm and obfuscated phrasing, rather than relying on keyword lists. The team has budget for a single transformer-based component and wants the strongest contextual understanding of natural language.

Which AI technique should the architect select?

choices.text: A large language model trained on broad natural-language corpora, used to score the semantic intent of each message.
choices.explanation: LLMs leverage transformer attention over large corpora to model contextual meaning, including idiom and obfuscation.

choices.text: A generative adversarial network with a generator that produces phishing samples and a discriminator that classifies them.
choices.explanation: GANs are designed for generating realistic synthetic data, not for nuanced text classification of inbound messages.

choices.text: A statistical learning model using term frequency-inverse document frequency vectors and logistic regression.
choices.explanation: TF-IDF treats words as independent tokens and cannot capture context, sarcasm, or obfuscated phrasing.

choices.text: A small language model fine-tuned only on the company's last quarter of internal email metadata.
choices.explanation: An SLM trained narrowly on metadata sacrifices the broad language understanding the requirement specifies.

questions.tip: Match the technique to the depth of language understanding required.
questions.explanation:
Transformer-based LLMs are purpose-built to capture contextual semantics across long natural-language inputs.

**Why it works:** Attention layers weight tokens in relation to one another, so meaning is derived from context rather than isolated keywords.

**Why the others don't work:**
- GAN: Aimed at synthetic data generation, not semantic classification.
- TF-IDF and logistic regression: Bag-of-words approach with no contextual reasoning.
- Narrow SLM on metadata: Too constrained to interpret nuanced body text.

questions.question:
The data science group at a managed detection provider is fine-tuning an open-weight model so it runs on resource-constrained sensors at the network edge. They have already pruned redundant neurons, and now need to reduce the numerical precision of the weights from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers so the model fits in memory and runs faster on the sensor's hardware.

Which fine-tuning technique is being described?

choices.text: Quantization, which reduces the bit-width of weights and activations to shrink memory footprint and accelerate inference.
choices.explanation: Quantization specifically maps higher-precision weights to lower-precision integer representations.

choices.text: Increasing the number of training epochs so the model converges further on the original full-precision weights.
choices.explanation: More epochs improve fit but do not reduce model size or precision; they may even worsen edge deployability.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning from human feedback to align the model with operator preferences on the sensor.
choices.explanation: RLHF tunes behaviour against preference signals; it does not change weight precision.

choices.text: Federated learning across the sensor fleet so each device contributes gradient updates back to the central model.
choices.explanation: Federated learning distributes training; it does not by itself reduce numerical precision.

questions.tip: Focus on what changes about the model's numerical representation, not its training data flow.
questions.explanation:
Reducing weight precision to fit constrained hardware is the textbook definition of quantization.

**Why it works:** Lower-precision integer math uses less memory and runs faster on edge accelerators.

**Why the others don't work:**
- More epochs: Improve convergence but not size or speed.
- RLHF: Aligns behaviour, not weight precision.
- Federated learning: Distributes training, not compression.

questions.question:
A SOC analyst is iterating on a prompt that asks an internal LLM to triage suspicious login events. The analyst includes three labelled examples of benign and three labelled examples of malicious events directly inside the prompt, followed by the new event to classify. No model weights are updated between calls.

Which prompt engineering pattern is the analyst applying?

choices.text: Multi-shot prompting, providing several worked examples in-context to steer the model's classification of a new input.
choices.explanation: Multi-shot (few-shot) prompting embeds multiple labelled exemplars in the prompt to guide the response.

choices.text: Zero-shot prompting, because the model has never seen labelled login event data during training.
choices.explanation: Zero-shot means no exemplars are provided in the prompt; the analyst is providing six.

choices.text: Fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, because the examples are teaching the model new triage behaviour.
choices.explanation: Fine-tuning updates model weights; in-context examples do not modify the model.

choices.text: One-shot prompting, providing a single labelled example to anchor the model's output format.
choices.explanation: One-shot uses exactly one exemplar; six exemplars qualify as multi-shot.

questions.tip: Count how many labelled exemplars sit inside the prompt itself.
questions.explanation:
Embedding multiple labelled exemplars in the prompt to guide a new prediction is multi-shot prompting.

**Why it works:** The model uses the in-context examples as soft demonstrations of the desired mapping from input to verdict.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Zero-shot: Provides no exemplars at all.
- Fine-tuning: Changes weights, not just the prompt.
- One-shot: Uses exactly one exemplar.

questions.question:
A regional bank is rolling out an AI assistant that will summarise customer support tickets. Compliance requires that the assistant always refuses to disclose internal account numbers and that it responds in a consistent professional tone, regardless of how the customer service agent phrases the request. The lead engineer is designing the prompt strategy.

Which TWO actions should the engineer take to enforce these requirements?

choices.text: Define a system prompt that pins the assistant's role, tone, and disclosure constraints before any user prompt is processed.
choices.explanation: The system prompt establishes persistent guardrails and persona that apply to every user turn.

choices.text: Use templated user prompts that pass agent input through fixed scaffolding around the variable ticket text.
choices.explanation: Templates ensure consistent framing of the user prompt and prevent ad-hoc phrasing from bypassing safeguards.

choices.text: Have each agent freely rephrase requests in natural language so the model receives diverse training-style examples.
choices.explanation: Unbounded free-form prompts increase the risk of jailbreaks and inconsistent behaviour, undermining the compliance goal.

choices.text: Quantize the underlying model to 4-bit weights so disallowed strings are pruned from memory.
choices.explanation: Quantization reduces precision but does not enforce content policy or persona constraints.

choices.text: Rely on zero-shot prompting with no system role, trusting the base model's pre-training to refuse appropriately.
choices.explanation: Without a system role, refusal behaviour is unreliable and inconsistent across phrasing.

questions.tip: Think about which layers of the prompt remain constant across every interaction.
questions.explanation:
Persistent behaviour is enforced by anchoring the model's role with a system prompt and constraining the variable input through templates.

**Why it works:** The system prompt sets immutable policy; templates ensure user input is wrapped in known scaffolding so the policy is never bypassed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Free-form rephrasing: Removes consistency and invites prompt injection.
- Quantization: Has nothing to do with content policy.
- Zero-shot with no system role: No guardrails are anchored.

questions.question: Match each AI type or training technique to the cybersecurity use case it best fits.

choices.text: Producing synthetic phishing emails to stress-test a detection model by pitting a generator against a discriminator
choices.explanation: GANs train two networks in opposition, with the generator producing samples and the discriminator judging them.

choices.text: Training a fraud model across many banks without any institution sharing its raw transaction data
choices.explanation: Federated learning keeps data local and aggregates model updates centrally, preserving data residency.

choices.text: Teaching an autonomous response agent to choose containment actions by rewarding successful incident outcomes
choices.explanation: Reinforcement learning learns a policy via reward signals tied to action outcomes in an environment.

choices.text: Running a compact language model directly on an endpoint to redact sensitive content offline
choices.explanation: SLMs trade breadth for footprint, making them suitable for on-device inference where resources are limited.

questions.tip: Identify the defining mechanism of each technique, not just its general AI category.
questions.explanation: Each technique maps to a different problem shape: adversarial data synthesis, decentralised training, policy learning by reward, and constrained on-device inference.

skills: 1.2: Explain the importance of data security in relation to AI.
questions.question:
A data engineer is preparing a training corpus for a fraud-detection model. Spot checks reveal duplicated rows, fields with leading and trailing whitespace, and several thousand records where the amount column contains the literal string null instead of a numeric value. Leadership wants these issues fixed before any model training begins so the model does not learn from corrupted inputs.

Which data processing activity directly addresses these findings?

choices.text: Data cleansing, which removes duplicates and normalises or repairs malformed values before the data is used downstream.
choices.explanation: Cleansing is the canonical step for de-duplication, whitespace trimming, and handling sentinel values.

choices.text: Data provenance, which records where each record originated and how it has been transformed.
choices.explanation: Provenance documents history but does not itself repair malformed values.

choices.text: Data augmentation, which synthesises additional records to expand the training set.
choices.explanation: Augmentation grows the dataset; it does not clean existing dirty records.

choices.text: Data balancing, which adjusts the ratio between fraudulent and legitimate samples.
choices.explanation: Balancing rebalances class distribution; it does not fix duplicates or null literals.

questions.tip: Focus on the activity that repairs malformed values rather than tracking or reshaping the dataset.
questions.explanation:
Cleansing is the explicit data processing step that handles malformed values, duplicates, and inconsistent formatting.

**Why it works:** Cleansing pipelines apply de-duplication, normalisation, and type-coercion rules so downstream training sees clean inputs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Provenance: Tracks origin and transformations but does not repair data.
- Augmentation: Generates new samples, not fixes existing ones.
- Balancing: Adjusts class ratios, not field-level quality.

questions.question:
Following a regulator's request, an AI governance officer must demonstrate, for every record that influenced a credit-scoring model, the original source system, the ingestion pipeline, every transformation step, and the engineer who approved each step. Internal audit also wants to confirm that no record was silently mutated after ingestion.

Which data processing concept satisfies this request?

choices.text: Data lineage, which captures the end-to-end path of a record from source through each transformation to its training-set destination.
choices.explanation: Lineage produces the auditable chain the regulator and auditors are asking for.

choices.text: Data cleansing, which standardises and repairs records before training.
choices.explanation: Cleansing improves quality but does not record the audit trail of transformations.

choices.text: Data balancing, which equalises class distributions across the training set.
choices.explanation: Balancing addresses class skew, not origin tracking.

choices.text: Data augmentation, which synthesises additional records to extend coverage.
choices.explanation: Augmentation creates new data; it does not document the lifecycle of existing data.

questions.tip: Identify the concept that produces an auditable transformation trail.
questions.explanation:
Lineage is the discipline of tracing every transformation applied to a record from its source to its final training use.

**Why it works:** A lineage graph lets auditors reconstruct exactly how each value reached the model and who approved each step.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cleansing: Improves quality but is not an audit trail.
- Balancing: Reshapes class distribution.
- Augmentation: Adds new synthetic samples.

questions.question:
The product team is launching a retrieval-augmented generation assistant that answers questions about thousands of internal incident reports. The reports are stored as long-form prose, and the team needs the assistant to look up semantically relevant passages at query time rather than relying only on what the base model memorised. The architect is selecting the storage layer.

Which component is required to support semantic retrieval over the reports?

choices.text: A vector store that holds embeddings of each report chunk, allowing nearest-neighbour search against the query embedding.
choices.explanation: RAG depends on vector storage of embeddings to enable similarity-based retrieval of relevant context.

choices.text: A relational database with full-text indexes on the report body, queried by exact keyword matches.
choices.explanation: Keyword full-text search misses semantic matches that share meaning but not vocabulary.

choices.text: A document store that returns reports in chronological order so the latest incidents are always retrieved first.
choices.explanation: Recency ordering does not surface semantically relevant context for the user's question.

choices.text: A blob store of the raw report files, with retrieval driven by the original filename pattern.
choices.explanation: Filename-based retrieval ignores the content of the reports entirely.

questions.tip: Consider what enables similarity search by meaning rather than by exact terms.
questions.explanation:
RAG retrieval relies on embeddings stored in a vector index so the system can find semantically similar passages.

**Why it works:** Query and document embeddings live in the same vector space; nearest-neighbour search returns conceptually related passages even when wording differs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Full-text keyword DB: Misses semantic synonyms.
- Chronological doc store: Recency, not relevance.
- Blob store by filename: No content awareness.

questions.question:
A media company's legal team wants to make it possible to prove later, with high confidence, that a given image was produced by the company's generative model. The marking must survive routine resizing and recompression and must not be visible to consumers viewing the image.

Which data security technique meets this requirement?

choices.text: Watermarking the generated images with an imperceptible signal that can be detected later to attribute provenance.
choices.explanation: Robust watermarking is designed to survive common transformations and to be detectable after the fact.

choices.text: Encrypting every output image at rest with a customer-managed key tied to the model identifier.
choices.explanation: Encryption protects storage confidentiality but is removed at viewing time, leaving nothing to prove origin.

choices.text: Hashing each output image and publishing the digest to an internal log accessible only to engineering.
choices.explanation: A hash changes after resize or recompression and cannot be recovered from the displayed image.

choices.text: Augmenting the training set with company-specific samples so the model's outputs include a recognisable visual style.
choices.explanation: A style is not a reliable forensic signal and is easily mimicked or stripped.

questions.tip: Focus on a marker that is invisible, robust to common edits, and recoverable later.
questions.explanation:
Imperceptible watermarking embeds a recoverable signal directly in the output, persisting through standard transformations.

**Why it works:** Detection algorithms recover the embedded signal even after resizing or recompression, supporting provenance claims.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Encryption: Removed at view time, no surviving marker.
- Hashing: Breaks on any edit.
- Style augmentation: Aesthetic, not forensic.

questions.question:
The data science group is preparing a labelled dataset of network flows for a model that classifies traffic as benign or malicious. Initial profiling shows 98 percent benign flows and 2 percent malicious, and several fields are populated inconsistently between sensor types. Before training begins, the team must address both the class skew and the quality issues so the model does not memorise the majority class or learn from malformed records.

Which TWO data processing activities should the team perform?

choices.text: Apply data balancing to adjust the ratio of malicious to benign flows so the minority class is adequately represented during training.
choices.explanation: Balancing directly addresses extreme class skew that would otherwise bias the model toward the majority.

choices.text: Apply data cleansing across the sensor-derived fields to normalise representations and repair malformed values.
choices.explanation: Cleansing fixes inconsistent field encodings between sensor types before features are extracted.

choices.text: Skip preprocessing and let the model learn the natural distribution since real traffic is genuinely skewed.
choices.explanation: Allowing severe skew without mitigation typically produces a model that always predicts benign.

choices.text: Quantize the dataset to 8-bit integer features so the model trains faster on the imbalanced data.
choices.explanation: Quantization is a model technique, not a data quality or balancing fix.

choices.text: Watermark every malicious flow so the model can learn to recognise the embedded signal.
choices.explanation: Watermarking is for output attribution, not for input-side class balance or cleansing.

questions.tip: Treat class skew and quality issues as two distinct problems that require their own remedies.
questions.explanation:
Class skew is addressed by balancing, and inconsistent field-level data is addressed by cleansing. Both are needed prior to training.

**Why it works:** Balancing prevents majority-class collapse; cleansing prevents the model from learning from corrupted features.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Skipping preprocessing: Produces a degenerate classifier.
- Quantization: Wrong layer of the stack.
- Watermarking: Output attribution, not input quality.

questions.question: Match each data category or concept to the example that best represents it.

choices.text: Rows of customer records in a relational table with fixed columns and types
choices.explanation: Relational tables with a defined schema are the canonical example of structured data.

choices.text: JSON event logs whose top-level keys are consistent but whose nested fields vary by event type
choices.explanation: Tagged but variable formats like JSON or XML are semi-structured.

choices.text: Free-form analyst incident write-ups stored as long prose documents
choices.explanation: Prose documents have no enforced schema and qualify as unstructured.

choices.text: Dense numerical vectors representing the semantic meaning of a document chunk
choices.explanation: Embeddings are learned vector representations used for similarity search in RAG pipelines.

questions.tip: Distinguish data by how much enforced schema each example carries.
questions.explanation: Structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data differ in schema enforcement; embeddings are a separate concept that represents content as vectors for retrieval.

skills: 1.3: Explain the importance of security throughout the life cycle of AI.
questions.question:
During the data collection phase for a healthcare triage model, a vendor offers to sell millions of pre-scraped patient narratives at very low cost. The data scientist cannot verify how the data was originally captured, whether patients consented, or whether any records have been altered since scraping. Leadership is pressing for speed of delivery.

Which life cycle concern should the data scientist raise as the primary blocker?

choices.text: The dataset's trustworthiness and authenticity cannot be established, so any model trained on it inherits unverified provenance and consent risk.
choices.explanation: Without verifiable authenticity, downstream model behaviour and legal posture are both unsupported.

choices.text: The dataset is too small to train a healthcare model, regardless of where it came from.
choices.explanation: Millions of narratives is not a size problem; the issue is integrity of source, not volume.

choices.text: The dataset will need to be quantized before it can be used for fine-tuning the triage model.
choices.explanation: Quantization is a model optimisation step, unrelated to source trustworthiness.

choices.text: The dataset must be augmented with synthetic samples before any evaluation can be run.
choices.explanation: Augmentation does not resolve the underlying provenance and consent concerns.

questions.tip: Focus on whether the source can be relied on, independent of size or downstream tuning.
questions.explanation:
Trustworthiness and authenticity of collected data are foundational to every later life cycle stage, especially in regulated domains.

**Why it works:** If you cannot establish how the data was captured and that it has not been altered, every downstream decision built on it is suspect.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Size: Not the stated problem.
- Quantization: Wrong concept and stage.
- Augmentation: Cannot fix a tainted source.

questions.question:
The CISO of a logistics company is reviewing a proposal to build an AI assistant that automatically reroutes drivers. The proposal lists technical metrics like inference latency and embedding dimensions but never explains how rerouting decisions will support the company's published goals of on-time delivery and driver safety. The CISO sends it back for revision.

Which AI life cycle activity is the proposal missing?

choices.text: Defining the business use case so the AI initiative is explicitly aligned with corporate objectives before development begins.
choices.explanation: Use case alignment ensures the project solves a business problem rather than chasing technical novelty.

choices.text: Selecting a small language model and fine-tuning it for low-latency edge inference.
choices.explanation: Model selection cannot happen meaningfully before the business problem is defined.

choices.text: Running model evaluation against held-out validation data and reporting precision and recall.
choices.explanation: Evaluation comes after a model exists; the gap is at the very start of the life cycle.

choices.text: Deploying the assistant in shadow mode behind the existing dispatch system.
choices.explanation: Shadow deployment is a later-stage tactic and presupposes a defined use case.

questions.tip: Ask what must be agreed before any technical work has value.
questions.explanation:
Every AI life cycle begins with an articulated business use case tied to corporate objectives; without it, downstream technical choices have no anchor.

**Why it works:** Aligning the use case with corporate objectives gives every later stage a measurable target.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model selection: Premature without a defined problem.
- Evaluation: Cannot evaluate against undefined goals.
- Shadow deployment: Operational stage, not strategic.

questions.question:
A SOC has deployed an LLM-based triage assistant that recommends a containment action for each new alert. Compliance requires that no host is isolated and no account is disabled purely on the model's recommendation. An analyst must review the recommendation, accept or override it, and click confirm before any change takes effect.

Which human-centric design principle does this workflow implement?

choices.text: Human-in-the-loop, because a person must approve each model recommendation before any action is taken.
choices.explanation: HITL inserts a mandatory human approval step in the action path.

choices.text: Human oversight, because senior leadership reviews aggregate model performance every quarter.
choices.explanation: Periodic governance reviews are oversight; the workflow described is per-decision approval.

choices.text: Human validation, because data scientists validate the training corpus before each model release.
choices.explanation: Validation of training data sits earlier in the life cycle and is not the per-alert control described.

choices.text: Autonomous response, because the analyst is informed of the action after it has executed.
choices.explanation: The scenario explicitly requires approval before action, which is the opposite of autonomous response.

questions.tip: Distinguish per-decision approval from periodic governance.
questions.explanation:
When a human must approve each individual model decision before it takes effect, that is the definition of human-in-the-loop.

**Why it works:** The mandatory approval step keeps the human inside the control loop for every action.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Human oversight: Operates at a governance cadence, not per decision.
- Human validation: Concerns training data, not runtime actions.
- Autonomous response: Removes the human, contradicting the requirement.

questions.question:
Three months after deploying a phishing-classifier model, the security team notices the false negative rate has slowly climbed from 2 percent to 7 percent. The training data and model have not changed, but attacker phrasing and lure styles have evolved. Stakeholders ask which life cycle activity should have detected this and which should now drive the fix.

Which combination of life cycle activities applies?

choices.text: Ongoing monitoring and maintenance should have surfaced the drift, and feedback and iteration should now drive a retraining cycle with updated samples.
choices.explanation: Drift detection is a monitoring responsibility; closing the loop with new data is the iteration step.

choices.text: Initial model evaluation should have prevented the drift, and a one-off cleansing pass should now restore performance.
choices.explanation: Pre-release evaluation cannot anticipate future attacker behaviour; cleansing does not address drift.

choices.text: Data collection should have been larger originally, and the model should now be quantized to recover accuracy.
choices.explanation: Quantization reduces precision and does not address concept drift.

choices.text: Business use case alignment should have prevented the issue, and the model should now be retired without replacement.
choices.explanation: The use case is still valid; retirement without replacement abandons the control rather than fixing it.

questions.tip: Match the detection responsibility to the stage that runs continuously, and the remediation to the stage that updates the model.
questions.explanation:
Post-deployment performance erosion is the textbook output of monitoring; the response is to iterate on training data and retrain.

**Why it works:** Monitoring observes runtime behaviour; feedback and iteration close the loop by feeding observed changes back into model updates.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Pre-release evaluation: Cannot foresee future drift.
- Bigger initial dataset and quantization: Wrong remedies.
- Retirement: Abandons rather than maintains the control.

skills: 1.3: Explain the importance of security throughout the life cycle of AI.
questions.question:
The model evaluation stage for a new insider-threat classifier is being designed. Stakeholders require that the team be able to defend, in front of an internal ethics board, both the model's measured accuracy on representative inputs and the appropriateness of its behaviour on edge cases that were never in the training data. The lead is choosing controls for this stage.

Which TWO controls should the evaluation stage include?

choices.text: Quantitative evaluation against a held-out, representative test set with documented precision, recall, and false positive metrics.
choices.explanation: Held-out evaluation produces the defensible metrics the ethics board will require.

choices.text: Human validation of model behaviour on curated edge cases that probe ethically sensitive scenarios.
choices.explanation: Human validation surfaces qualitative issues that aggregate metrics miss.

choices.text: Skipping evaluation in non-production and instead relying on real-world outcomes once the model is deployed.
choices.explanation: Production-only learning forfeits the chance to catch issues before harm occurs.

choices.text: Quantizing the model to reduce inference cost before any evaluation metrics are gathered.
choices.explanation: Quantization is an optimisation, not an evaluation control, and may itself change measured behaviour.

choices.text: Replacing the test set with samples generated by the model itself to demonstrate self-consistency.
choices.explanation: Self-generated tests measure consistency, not correctness, and bias the result toward the model's own distribution.

questions.tip: Pair a quantitative measurement with a qualitative human check.
questions.explanation:
Robust evaluation combines metric-driven testing on a held-out set with human validation on sensitive edge cases.

**Why it works:** Together they cover both measurable performance and qualitative appropriateness, which is what an ethics board expects.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Skipping evaluation: Defers detection to production harm.
- Quantization first: Confuses optimisation with evaluation.
- Self-generated tests: Circular and biased.

questions.question: Arrange the following AI life cycle stages in the correct order for a new fraud-detection initiative.

choices.text: Define the business use case and align the initiative with corporate fraud-reduction objectives
choices.explanation: Use case definition anchors every subsequent decision in a stated business goal.

choices.text: Collect and prepare the data, verifying source trustworthiness and addressing quality and balance issues
choices.explanation: Data collection and preparation precede modelling so the model trains on trustworthy inputs.

choices.text: Develop and select the candidate model, then evaluate it against held-out data and human-reviewed edge cases
choices.explanation: Development, selection, and evaluation establish that the model meets the defined goals before release.

choices.text: Deploy the model into production behind appropriate human-in-the-loop controls
choices.explanation: Deployment exposes the model to real workloads under the agreed control regime.

choices.text: Monitor performance, capture feedback, and iterate on the model as conditions change
choices.explanation: Monitoring and iteration sustain model performance over time and close the life cycle loop.

questions.tip: Order the stages so that each step has the inputs the next one requires.

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, use AI threat-modeling resources.
questions.question:
A retail company is preparing to deploy a customer-facing chatbot built on a third-party large language model. The architecture team needs to enumerate the most relevant threats specific to generative AI workloads, including risks tied to user prompts, model outputs, and integrated plug-ins. The CISO has asked for a community-maintained list focused specifically on LLM-based applications rather than general web or ML risks.

Which resource should the architecture team consult first?

choices.text: The OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, which enumerates prompt injection, insecure output handling, and related LLM-specific risks.
choices.explanation: This list is purpose-built for LLM applications and covers exactly the threat categories the team needs to model.

choices.text: The OWASP Top 10 for Web Applications, which covers injection, broken access control, and traditional web risks.
choices.explanation: The web Top 10 predates generative AI and does not address prompt injection, training data poisoning, or model output handling.

choices.text: The OWASP Machine Learning Security Top 10, which focuses on classical supervised and unsupervised model risks.
choices.explanation: The ML Top 10 targets traditional ML pipelines, not the prompt and plug-in surfaces specific to LLM chat applications.

choices.text: The CVE database filtered for entries mentioning the model vendor over the past 12 months.
choices.explanation: CVEs catalog disclosed vulnerabilities in specific products but do not provide a structured threat-modeling taxonomy.

questions.tip: Match the resource scope to the type of AI system being threat modeled.
questions.explanation:
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is the dedicated community resource for threat modeling LLM-powered systems.

**Why it works:** It enumerates risks such as prompt injection, training data poisoning, insecure output handling, model denial of service, and excessive agency that are unique to LLM workloads.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Web Top 10: covers traditional web application risks, not LLM-specific surfaces.
- ML Top 10: targets classical ML pipelines such as model skewing and membership inference rather than generative LLM concerns.
- CVE search: lists product-specific defects, not a threat taxonomy.

The behavior includes probing the model with crafted inputs to extract training data and gradually poisoning a public dataset used for retraining. The lead needs a resource that aligns with the ATT&CK style of tactic and technique mapping but is purpose-built for AI systems.

Which framework should the lead use?

choices.text: MITRE ATLAS, which catalogs adversary tactics and techniques against AI-enabled systems in an ATT&CK-style matrix.
choices.explanation: ATLAS provides the structured tactic and technique taxonomy specifically for adversarial machine learning scenarios.

choices.text: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise matrix, mapping each behavior to TA0001 Initial Access techniques.
choices.explanation: ATT&CK Enterprise covers traditional IT adversary behaviors and does not include model evasion or training data poisoning techniques.

choices.text: The MIT AI Risk Repository, organizing risks by causal factor and domain.
choices.explanation: The MIT repository catalogs risks for research and policy work but is not an adversary tactics and techniques matrix.

choices.text: The CVE AI Working Group catalog of disclosed AI vulnerabilities.
choices.explanation: That group focuses on standardizing AI CVE entries, not on mapping adversary behaviors to tactics.

questions.tip: Identify the framework that mirrors ATT&CK structure but for AI systems.
questions.explanation:
MITRE ATLAS is the adversarial threat landscape for AI systems and uses the same tactic and technique structure as ATT&CK.

**Why it works:** It includes techniques such as ML model evasion, ML supply chain compromise, and model poisoning that directly match the observed behavior.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ATT&CK Enterprise: covers traditional intrusion tradecraft, not adversarial ML.
- MIT AI Risk Repository: a taxonomy of risks, not adversary techniques.
- CVE AI Working Group: standardizes vulnerability disclosure, not tactic mapping.

choices.explanation: The ML Top 10 directly targets the supervised tabular pipeline being threat modeled.

choices.text: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, treating each feature as a potential prompt injection vector.

questions.tip: Pick the resource whose scope matches classical ML rather than LLM workloads.
questions.explanation:
The OWASP ML Security Top 10 is scoped to classical ML pipelines and their failure modes.

**Why it works:** It enumerates training data poisoning, model serialization, transfer learning attacks, and input manipulation, which match the in-scope pipeline.

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, use AI threat-modeling resources.

Which resource is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: MITRE ATLAS, which focuses on adversary tactics targeting AI systems.

questions.explanation:
The MIT AI Risk Repository is a multi-domain catalog of AI risks suited to executive policy briefings.

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, use AI threat-modeling resources.
questions.question:
The security architect is threat modeling a new AI-powered code review assistant that uses an external LLM and a retrieval augmented generation pipeline drawing from private source repositories. The architect wants to use community resources to enumerate both the application-layer LLM risks and the adversary techniques an attacker might chain against the model. The goal is a defensible threat model that combines an application risk taxonomy with an attacker tactic and technique matrix.

Which TWO resources should the architect combine for this exercise?

choices.text: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications to enumerate application-layer LLM risks such as prompt injection and sensitive information disclosure.
choices.explanation: It provides the application risk taxonomy for the LLM-based assistant.

choices.text: MITRE ATLAS to map adversary tactics and techniques targeting the AI system from reconnaissance through impact.
choices.explanation: ATLAS supplies the attacker tactic and technique matrix the architect requires.

choices.text: The OWASP Mobile Top 10 to catalog client-side risks of the IDE plug-in.
choices.explanation: The mobile Top 10 targets mobile app risks, not the AI threat model.

choices.text: ISO 27001 Annex A controls, treating each control as a threat category.
choices.explanation: ISO 27001 is a management system standard, not a threat enumeration framework.

choices.text: The PCI DSS scoping guidance to define the AI system's data flow.
choices.explanation: PCI DSS scoping applies to cardholder data environments, not LLM threat modeling.

questions.tip: Combine an application risk taxonomy with an adversary tactics matrix.
questions.explanation:
Pairing the OWASP LLM Top 10 with MITRE ATLAS gives both the application-layer risk view and the adversary technique view that a complete threat model needs.

**Why it works:** The LLM Top 10 frames what can go wrong in the application; ATLAS frames how an adversary would attempt to make it go wrong, with tactics from reconnaissance to impact.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Mobile Top 10: wrong application class.
- ISO 27001: a controls framework, not a threat taxonomy.
- PCI DSS scoping: payment data scoping, not AI threats.
