skills: 2.2: Given a set of requirements, implement security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
The product team is launching a customer support assistant built on a third-party LLM. Marketing wants the assistant to refuse to discuss competitors, never reveal internal pricing logic, and always respond in the customer's language. The security architect needs a control that ships these constraints with every request without relying on the customer to phrase the question safely.

Which control should the architect implement?

choices.text: Wrap every user message with a server-side prompt template that injects the persona, refusal rules, and language policy as system instructions before forwarding to the model.
choices.explanation: A server-side prompt template enforces the constraints on every call, independent of user input.

choices.text: Document the constraints in the customer-facing help center and rely on user education.
choices.explanation: User education does not stop malicious or careless prompts from bypassing the rules.

choices.text: Allow customers to choose a system prompt from a dropdown of options before each session.
choices.explanation: Letting clients pick or modify the system prompt lets them disable the very constraints the business requires.

choices.text: Train a custom model from scratch using only sanitized internal data.
choices.explanation: Training a new base model is disproportionate, slow, and does not address per-request policy enforcement.

questions.tip: Think about where the policy is enforced relative to the user.
questions.explanation:
A server-side prompt template is the standard control for binding policy to every model call.

**Why it works:** The template prepends trusted system instructions on the server before the user prompt is sent, so refusal rules and persona constraints cannot be skipped or edited by the client.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Help center docs: rely on user behavior.
- Client-selected prompts: removes the control surface from the operator.
- Train from scratch: disproportionate and does not enforce per-request rules.

skills: 2.2: Given a set of requirements, implement security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
During load testing, the operations team observes that a small number of API keys are consuming nearly all of the LLM inference budget. The provider charges per token, and the requirement states that any single tenant must be capped at a fixed number of tokens per minute regardless of how many requests it sends. The team needs a gateway control that ties throttling to consumption rather than just request count.

Which control should the team enable?

choices.text: Configure token-per-minute limits on the gateway, scoped per API key, so the gateway tracks input plus output tokens and rejects requests once the cap is reached.
choices.explanation: Token limits cap consumption directly and match the requirement.

choices.text: Enable requests-per-minute rate limiting on the gateway, scoped per source IP.
choices.explanation: Request-per-minute limits cap call frequency but do not control token consumption, and IP scoping misses shared egress.

choices.text: Add a per-request maximum tokens parameter only, without any per-key aggregate limit.
choices.explanation: Capping a single response does nothing to stop a tenant from sending many capped responses back-to-back.

choices.text: Set CPU limits on the inference servers using container quotas.
choices.explanation: CPU quotas do not map to per-tenant token consumption or to the billing-driven requirement.

questions.tip: Match the unit of consumption to the unit being controlled.
questions.explanation:
Token-per-minute limits scoped per API key are the gateway control that maps directly to the requirement.

**Why it works:** The gateway aggregates input and output tokens per key and enforces a ceiling that matches the billing model.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RPM by IP: throttles requests, not tokens, and IP scope is unreliable.
- Per-request max tokens: does not limit aggregate use.
- CPU quotas: infrastructure metric, not tenant token consumption.

skills: 2.2: Given a set of requirements, implement security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
A healthcare provider is exposing a multimodal model that accepts text and images. The security requirement is to block uploads of audio and video, refuse documents larger than 5 MB, and limit each request to a single image. The architect wants this enforced before any data reaches the model or inference cluster.

Which control set should the architect implement at the AI gateway?

choices.text: Configure modality limits to allow only text and image inputs, an input quota capping payload size at 5 MB, and a per-request image count of one.
choices.explanation: These gateway controls match each part of the requirement and run before the model is invoked.

choices.text: Rely on the model's own refusal behavior to decline audio and video requests.
choices.explanation: Letting the model decide wastes inference and depends on unreliable model behavior for a hard input rule.

choices.text: Apply only a 5 MB payload size limit at the load balancer and accept any modality the model supports.
choices.explanation: A single size limit does not enforce modality or per-request image counts.

choices.text: Configure prompt templates that ask the user not to upload audio or video.
choices.explanation: Templates do not block uploads at the transport or gateway layer.

questions.tip: Place hard input rules at the gateway, not the model.
questions.explanation:
Modality limits, input quotas, and per-request counts are gateway controls designed exactly for shaping accepted inputs.

**Why it works:** They reject non-conforming requests before tokens are spent on inference and before potentially harmful payloads reach the model.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model refusal: unreliable and wasteful.
- Single size limit: misses modality and count rules.
- Prompt templates: do not block uploads.

skills: 2.2: Given a set of requirements, implement security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
The red team has reported that the deployed prompt firewall sometimes lets through obfuscated jailbreak attempts hidden inside multi-step reasoning prompts. Engineering wants ongoing assurance that the guardrails actually catch the attack classes they claim to. Leadership has asked for a repeatable process, not a one-time penetration test.

Which practice should engineering adopt?

choices.text: Implement automated guardrail testing using a regression suite of known jailbreak, injection, and policy-violating prompts that runs on every guardrail change.
choices.explanation: A regression suite gives repeatable, ongoing validation of the guardrails' effectiveness.

choices.text: Schedule a quarterly manual penetration test against the chatbot.
choices.explanation: Quarterly testing is point-in-time and does not catch regressions between tests.

choices.text: Replace the prompt firewall with a stricter system prompt and accept some user friction.
choices.explanation: Tightening the system prompt is a control change, not a validation practice.

choices.text: Capture user feedback when they report unsafe replies.
choices.explanation: User reports are reactive and miss attacks that succeed quietly.

questions.tip: Match the requirement for ongoing assurance to a repeatable automated test process.
questions.explanation:
Automated guardrail regression testing provides continuous validation of policy enforcement.

**Why it works:** A maintained suite of adversarial prompts runs in CI and catches regressions whenever templates, models, or firewall rules change.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Quarterly pentest: point-in-time.
- Stricter prompt: a change, not validation.
- User feedback: reactive and incomplete.

skills: 2.2: Given a set of requirements, implement security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
Architecture is finalizing the security controls for a public LLM endpoint that supports text only. The requirements call for blocking known prompt injection patterns inline, capping how quickly any one client can call the model, and stopping any client from spending an entire month's token budget in a day. The team has no requirement to filter image content or to restrict outbound responses by length.

Which TWO gateway controls satisfy the stated requirements?

choices.text: Deploy a prompt firewall that inspects incoming prompts and blocks known injection and jailbreak patterns before they reach the model.
choices.explanation: It directly satisfies the inline injection-blocking requirement.

choices.text: Configure per-client rate limits and daily token quotas at the gateway so a single tenant cannot exhaust the monthly budget.
choices.explanation: This satisfies both the rate and aggregate consumption requirements.

choices.text: Restrict accepted modalities to disallow audio and video uploads.
choices.explanation: Modality restriction is unnecessary because the endpoint is text only.

choices.text: Enforce a maximum response token length on every reply to keep answers short.
choices.explanation: There is no requirement to cap output length.

choices.text: Configure regional geo-blocking at the CDN to deny traffic from selected countries.
choices.explanation: Geo-blocking is not part of the stated requirements.

questions.tip: Pick controls that map one-to-one to each stated requirement.
questions.explanation:
A prompt firewall handles injection inspection, and per-client rate plus token quotas handle the consumption ceilings.

**Why it works:** Each control addresses one of the explicit requirements at the gateway, before reaching the model.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Modality limits, output length caps, and geo-blocking are not in scope.

skills: 2.2: Given a set of requirements, implement security controls for AI systems.
questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order for designing and validating security controls around a new LLM-powered application.

choices.text: Capture the security requirements from policy, compliance, and business stakeholders for the AI workload
choices.explanation: Requirements drive every later design and validation decision.

choices.text: Map each requirement to specific model, gateway, and prompt template controls
choices.explanation: Mapping ensures every requirement has a concrete enforcement point.

choices.text: Implement the controls in the gateway and model configuration
choices.explanation: Implementation follows the design and mapping phase.

choices.text: Run guardrail testing and validation against an adversarial prompt suite and tune until coverage is acceptable
choices.explanation: Validation confirms the controls actually satisfy the requirements.

questions.tip: Requirements come before design, design before implementation, and validation last.
questions.explanation: Security control design for AI systems follows the same requirements-design-implement-validate progression as other security work.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, implement appropriate access controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
An internal LLM endpoint hosts both a general assistant and a fine-tuned legal model that may only be used by the legal department. Engineering currently fronts the endpoint with a shared API key, and the team needs to ensure only authorized users can invoke each model. Audit also requires the identity of the calling user to appear in inference logs.

Which access control approach should the team implement?

choices.text: Replace the shared key with per-user OAuth tokens and authorize each request against a model-level policy that grants the legal model only to members of the legal group.
choices.explanation: Per-user tokens plus model-level authorization satisfy both least privilege and audit.

choices.text: Keep the shared key and rely on prompt instructions telling the legal model to refuse other departments.
choices.explanation: A shared key removes user identity, and prompt-based refusals are unreliable for access control.

choices.text: Issue a second shared key for the legal model and email it to the legal team.
choices.explanation: A second shared key still loses individual identity and is easy to leak.

choices.text: Allow any authenticated employee to call any model and review usage monthly in a report.
choices.explanation: After-the-fact review is not an access control and does not satisfy least privilege.

questions.tip: Think about authentication of individuals and authorization scoped per model.
questions.explanation:
Per-user authentication combined with model-level authorization implements least privilege and supports auditable logs.

**Why it works:** Identity propagates into the inference logs, and the policy decision binds model access to group membership.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Shared key plus refusal prompt: no identity, weak enforcement.
- Second shared key: no per-user identity.
- Open access plus review: monitoring is not access control.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, implement appropriate access controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
A retrieval augmented generation pipeline indexes documents from multiple business units into a shared vector store. Users have been receiving answers that quote documents from units they are not authorized to read. The product owner needs an access control approach that preserves the existing source system permissions when documents are retrieved during generation.

Which control should the architect implement?

choices.text: Apply document-level access controls during retrieval, filtering the vector store by the caller's identity and group membership before passing context to the model.
choices.explanation: Identity-aware retrieval enforces source system permissions at query time.

choices.text: Re-rank retrieved documents using the model's own assessment of relevance.
choices.explanation: Relevance re-ranking has no relationship to authorization.

choices.text: Encrypt the vector store at rest and grant the application service account broad read access.
choices.explanation: At-rest encryption does not stop authorized service accounts from returning unauthorized content.

choices.text: Append a system prompt asking the model not to quote documents from other business units.
choices.explanation: Prompt instructions are not a reliable access control for data the model has already received.

questions.tip: Enforce authorization at the data retrieval boundary, not in the prompt.
questions.explanation:
Identity-aware filtering at retrieval prevents unauthorized documents from ever entering the model context.

**Why it works:** It applies the same authorization model the source systems already enforce, scoped to the caller making the request.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Relevance re-ranking: unrelated to authorization.
- At-rest encryption: does not stop authorized retrieval.
- Prompt instructions: unreliable and after the fact.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, implement appropriate access controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
An autonomous agent built on an LLM has been granted tools that can read email, send email, schedule meetings, and post to internal chat. Security review flagged that any prompt injection could lead the agent to perform high-impact actions on behalf of the user. The team needs to reduce the blast radius without removing the assistant entirely.

Which access control should the team apply to the agent?

choices.text: Scope the agent's tool permissions to least privilege, granting only the tools the current task requires and requiring user confirmation for high-impact actions such as sending email.
choices.explanation: Least privilege plus a confirmation step limits the impact of any successful injection.

choices.text: Grant the agent the same broad permissions as the user so it can act seamlessly.
choices.explanation: Mirroring the user's full permissions maximizes blast radius rather than reducing it.

choices.text: Run the agent under a service account with admin rights to avoid permission errors.
choices.explanation: Admin rights are the opposite of least privilege and amplify impact.

choices.text: Hide the high-impact tools from the system prompt while leaving them callable.
choices.explanation: Hiding tools in the prompt does not stop a determined attacker from invoking them.

questions.tip: Limit what the agent is allowed to do, not what it is told it can do.
questions.explanation:
Least privilege agent tooling, combined with a human-in-the-loop step for sensitive actions, is the standard control to limit excessive agency.

**Why it works:** The agent simply does not have the capability to take high-impact actions without explicit confirmation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Broad user rights: maximizes blast radius.
- Admin service account: amplifies impact.
- Hidden tools: still invokable.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, implement appropriate access controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
The platform team exposes a model inference API to a partner over the public internet. The partner uses a single set of long-lived credentials shared across its developers. The security team has been asked to harden access to the API without changing the partner's developer workflow significantly.

Which control offers the BEST improvement?

choices.text: Restrict the API to the partner's published egress IP ranges and rotate the API credential on a defined schedule with documented compromise procedures.
choices.explanation: Network restriction plus credential rotation hardens the API access path without forcing per-developer onboarding.

choices.text: Remove all authentication and rely on the obscurity of the API URL.
choices.explanation: Security by obscurity is not an access control.

choices.text: Accept any TLS client certificate signed by a public certificate authority.
choices.explanation: Trusting any publicly issued certificate authenticates strangers, not the partner.

choices.text: Disable TLS to simplify partner integration and improve throughput.
choices.explanation: Disabling TLS removes confidentiality and integrity, weakening rather than hardening access.

questions.tip: Combine identity, network, and credential lifecycle controls at the API edge.
questions.explanation:
Restricting source networks and rotating credentials provides defense in depth at the API edge while preserving partner workflow.

**Why it works:** Source IP restrictions reduce exposure to scanning and brute force; rotation reduces the value of stolen credentials.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Obscurity: not a control.
- Any public CA: trusts the world.
- Disable TLS: removes a foundational protection.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, implement appropriate access controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
The security team is finalizing access controls for an internal AI assistant. Requirements specify that only authenticated employees can call the inference API, that each request must carry user identity for logging, and that the underlying training dataset must only be accessible to the data science team. The team must satisfy all three requirements with concrete controls.

Which TWO controls together satisfy the requirements?

choices.text: Enforce SSO-backed authentication and per-user authorization at the API gateway so every request carries an attributable identity.
choices.explanation: This handles both API authentication and user-identity logging.

choices.text: Apply IAM policies on the training data storage that restrict read access to members of the data science group.
choices.explanation: This isolates the training dataset to the appropriate team.

choices.text: Distribute a shared API key to all employees through a wiki page.
choices.explanation: Shared keys remove identity and weaken authentication.

choices.text: Make the training data bucket public to ease internal collaboration.
choices.explanation: Public access violates the data access requirement.

choices.text: Disable logging on the inference API to reduce noise.
choices.explanation: Disabling logs eliminates the identity logging the requirement demands.

questions.tip: Pair an API-layer identity control with a data-layer authorization control.
questions.explanation:
SSO with per-user authorization covers the API surface, while IAM on the training data covers the data surface.

**Why it works:** Each requirement is enforced at the correct boundary, with the identity flowing through to logs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Shared keys: lose identity.
- Public data: contradicts the requirement.
- Disable logging: removes the audit trail.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, implement appropriate access controls for AI systems.
questions.question: Match each AI access control category to the example that best represents how it is enforced in practice.

choices.text: Policy that limits which users or groups may invoke a specific fine-tuned model variant
choices.explanation: Model access controls which identities can call a given model deployment.

choices.text: IAM rules on the feature store and training datasets that restrict read or write to authorized roles
choices.explanation: Data access governs the underlying datasets used to train and ground the model.

choices.text: Least privilege tool permissions granted to an autonomous assistant, with human confirmation for sensitive actions
choices.explanation: Agent access controls bound the capabilities and tool scope of the autonomous component.

choices.text: Gateway authentication, source IP allowlists, and per-key rate limits on the inference endpoint
choices.explanation: API access controls govern how external callers reach the inference endpoint.

questions.tip: Map each category to the layer where the control is enforced.
questions.explanation: Each access control category sits at a different layer: the model, the data, the agent's tooling, or the API edge. Mapping the example to the correct layer is the key to applying the right control.

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, implement data security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
The compliance team is reviewing how prompts and responses move between the customer browser, the application backend, and the third-party inference provider. Internal policy requires that no plaintext content is exposed on any network segment, including links between the application and the inference vendor. Engineering needs to confirm the encryption posture for each hop.

Which control set satisfies the policy?

choices.text: Terminate TLS at the customer-facing load balancer and use mutual TLS for the application-to-inference connection so every network hop is encrypted in transit.
choices.explanation: Encrypted client TLS plus mTLS to the inference provider covers every network segment.

choices.text: Encrypt requests at the client and pass them as plaintext over an internal HTTP link to the inference provider.
choices.explanation: Sending plaintext on any hop violates the policy regardless of earlier encryption.

choices.text: Use TLS only between the browser and the load balancer because backend networks are trusted.
choices.explanation: Backend trust is not equivalent to encryption, and the policy explicitly covers the vendor link.

choices.text: Tokenize each request payload and send the resulting opaque ID in plaintext over HTTP.
choices.explanation: Tokenization is not encryption and HTTP still exposes the token transit on the wire.

questions.tip: The policy is about transit on every hop, not just the client edge.
questions.explanation:
TLS for the client and mutual TLS to the inference vendor encrypt every network segment.

**Why it works:** Each hop is protected by a separate TLS session, including authentication of the vendor endpoint.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Backend plaintext: violates policy.
- TLS only at the edge: leaves backend hops exposed.
- Tokenization over HTTP: not encryption.

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, implement data security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
A financial institution wants to fine-tune a model on customer interaction transcripts, but compliance forbids the model from learning or memorizing account numbers, card numbers, or government identifiers. The data engineering team needs to transform the dataset before training so the model never sees those identifiers in any reconstructable form.

Which data safety control should the team apply?

choices.text: Redact identifiers from the training corpus before fine-tuning, removing the values entirely so they cannot be recovered by the model.
choices.explanation: Redaction destroys the sensitive values so the model cannot memorize them.

choices.text: Apply format-preserving masking that keeps the original values intact for downstream joins.
choices.explanation: Preserving the original values still feeds them to the model and risks memorization.

choices.text: Encrypt the training corpus at rest and feed the ciphertext to the trainer.
choices.explanation: Models cannot learn meaningful patterns from arbitrary ciphertext, and the data must be decrypted to train.

choices.text: Add a system prompt at inference time asking the model not to repeat identifiers.
choices.explanation: Inference-time instructions do not prevent training-time memorization.

questions.tip: If the model must never learn the value, the value must not be in the training data.
questions.explanation:
Redaction removes sensitive identifiers from the corpus so the model never sees them.

**Why it works:** Without the values present, the model cannot memorize or regurgitate them.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Format-preserving masking: still exposes real values if reversible or unchanged.
- Encrypt at rest: data must be decrypted for training.
- Inference instructions: do not address training-time memorization.

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, implement data security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
The research team has been collecting telemetry from a beta AI product and storing every field returned by the client, including precise GPS coordinates and device identifiers that are not used by any current model. Privacy review has asked the team to align collection with the principle of collecting only what is necessary for the stated purpose.

Which control should the team apply?

choices.text: Implement data minimization by changing the client and server schemas to collect only the fields required for the documented purposes.
choices.explanation: Minimization removes the unnecessary fields from the collection pipeline.

choices.text: Continue collecting every field and rely on retention policies to delete data later.
choices.explanation: Retention does not address over-collection at the source and increases exposure in the interim.

choices.text: Encrypt the GPS coordinates with a separate key and keep collecting them.
choices.explanation: Encryption does not reduce collection or align with minimization.

choices.text: Hash device identifiers and continue collecting precise GPS.
choices.explanation: Hashing identifiers does not address the unjustified collection of precise location.

questions.tip: If the data is not needed, the right answer is not to collect it.
questions.explanation:
Data minimization is the control for collecting only what is necessary.

**Why it works:** Removing the unnecessary fields reduces risk at the source and aligns with privacy principles.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Retention: addresses storage time, not collection scope.
- Encryption: protects confidentiality but does not reduce collection.
- Partial hashing: still over-collects location data.

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, implement data security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
A multi-tenant inference platform processes requests from customers in regulated industries. The platform owner needs to ensure that prompts and responses are protected even while they are being held in memory during inference, in case a co-tenant or compromised process could read the same memory pages. The platform already uses TLS in transit and disk encryption.

Which additional control addresses the requirement?

choices.text: Run inference inside confidential computing enclaves so prompts and responses remain encrypted in use within protected memory.
choices.explanation: Confidential computing addresses the in-use encryption gap.

choices.text: Increase the TLS cipher strength on the public endpoint.
choices.explanation: Stronger transit ciphers do not protect data already inside memory.

choices.text: Rotate the disk encryption keys more frequently.
choices.explanation: Disk key rotation protects data at rest, not data in use.

choices.text: Add a longer prompt template warning the model not to leak data.
choices.explanation: Prompt templates do not protect memory contents.

questions.tip: Match the state of the data to the encryption control: transit, rest, or use.
questions.explanation:
Confidential computing protects data in use by keeping it encrypted within hardware-backed enclaves.

**Why it works:** Even a co-tenant or compromised process outside the enclave cannot read the protected memory pages.

**Why the others don't work:**
- TLS cipher: transit only.
- Disk key rotation: rest only.
- Prompt template: not an encryption control.

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, implement data security controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
An analytics team is building a model that will be used for research only, where individual users do not need to be re-identified at any point. The privacy and security teams require both that any persistent identifiers are stripped from the dataset and that classifications make it clear which fields remain sensitive. They want the controls applied before the dataset leaves the source environment.

Which TWO controls together satisfy the requirements?

choices.text: Anonymize the dataset by removing direct identifiers and generalizing quasi-identifiers so individuals cannot be re-identified.
choices.explanation: Anonymization addresses the re-identification requirement.

choices.text: Apply data classification labels to each remaining field so consumers know its sensitivity and required handling.
choices.explanation: Classification labels communicate handling requirements downstream.

choices.text: Store the raw dataset unmodified and document the rules in a wiki page.
choices.explanation: Documentation alone does not transform the data and leaves identifiers in place.

choices.text: Mask only the display layer in the analytics dashboard.
choices.explanation: Display masking leaves the underlying dataset exposed.

choices.text: Encrypt the dataset with a key shared across all analysts.
choices.explanation: Shared-key encryption does not address re-identification or classification.

questions.tip: Combine an identity removal control with a labeling control.
questions.explanation:
Anonymization and classification labels together remove individual identification and communicate the sensitivity of what remains.

**Why it works:** The data leaves the source environment de-identified and tagged, supporting safe research use.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Wiki rules: no transformation.
- Display masking: dataset still exposed.
- Shared-key encryption: does not de-identify or classify.

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, implement data security controls for AI systems.
questions.question: Match each data safety control to the description that best fits how it protects an AI workload.

choices.text: Transforming the dataset so that individuals cannot be re-identified, often by removing direct identifiers and generalizing quasi-identifiers
choices.explanation: Anonymization aims to prevent re-identification of individuals.

choices.text: Removing sensitive values entirely from a document or transcript so they cannot be recovered
choices.explanation: Redaction removes content; the original values are gone from the artifact.

choices.text: Replacing sensitive values with format-preserving substitutes for display or non-production use
choices.explanation: Masking hides values while preserving format, often for testing or display.

choices.text: Collecting and retaining only the data fields necessary for the stated purpose
choices.explanation: Minimization governs how much data is collected and kept.

questions.tip: Distinguish removal of identity, removal of content, substitution, and reduction of scope.
questions.explanation: Each control addresses data risk at a different point: anonymization prevents re-identification, redaction removes specific values, masking substitutes them, and minimization reduces collection.

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, implement monitoring and auditing for AI systems.
questions.question:
Operations is rolling out logging for a customer-facing chatbot. The compliance team requires that prompts and responses be captured for forensic and audit use, but the privacy team has flagged that the same logs could contain customer-supplied PII. The team needs a way to retain useful operational and security signal in logs without storing raw sensitive content indefinitely.

Which control should operations implement?

choices.text: Sanitize prompt and response logs by redacting detected PII fields before write while keeping prompt and response metadata, identifiers, and policy decisions intact.
choices.explanation: Log sanitization preserves operational signal while removing the raw sensitive content.

choices.text: Disable prompt and response logging entirely to avoid privacy risk.
choices.explanation: Disabling the logs satisfies privacy by destroying the forensic signal compliance requires.

choices.text: Store the raw prompts and responses in a public bucket so any team can review them.
choices.explanation: Public storage of raw content is a serious privacy and security failure.

choices.text: Log only the model's confidence scores and discard prompt and response text.
choices.explanation: Confidence scores alone do not support forensic or audit use of the conversation content.

questions.tip: Find the control that reconciles forensic value with privacy.
questions.explanation:
Log sanitization redacts sensitive fields at write time while preserving the structure and metadata needed for auditing.

**Why it works:** It keeps logs useful for incident response and compliance reviews without storing raw PII.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disable logging: removes forensic signal.
- Public storage: privacy failure.
- Confidence only: insufficient detail.

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, implement monitoring and auditing for AI systems.
questions.question:
Finance has flagged that monthly inference spend on a hosted LLM has tripled without a corresponding increase in user count. Engineering needs to identify which tenants, features, and prompt patterns are driving the spend so the team can act on the largest contributors before the next billing cycle.

Which monitoring practice should engineering put in place?

choices.text: Instrument AI cost monitoring that attributes token spend per tenant, per feature, and per prompt template so the largest contributors can be ranked and addressed.
choices.explanation: Attributed cost monitoring directly identifies the dominant contributors to spend.

choices.text: Forward all inference logs to the SIEM without enrichment and review them weekly.
choices.explanation: Raw logs without attribution do not answer the per-tenant or per-feature question.

choices.text: Lower the per-request maximum tokens uniformly and assume cost will fall.
choices.explanation: Blind capping is a control, not a monitoring practice, and may degrade legitimate features.

choices.text: Track only the total monthly invoice amount from the inference vendor.
choices.explanation: Aggregate invoice values cannot be decomposed by tenant or feature.

questions.tip: Look for monitoring that breaks down spend along the dimensions you need to act on.
questions.explanation:
Attributed AI cost monitoring decomposes spend across the dimensions engineering needs to act on.

**Why it works:** Per-tenant, per-feature, and per-template cost views surface the dominant contributors.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Raw SIEM logs: no attribution.
- Blind token caps: a control, not monitoring.
- Invoice total: not decomposable.

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, implement monitoring and auditing for AI systems.
questions.question:
A clinical decision support assistant has been in production for six months. Leadership wants an audit that focuses specifically on whether the model is generating fabricated facts that look authoritative, even when it does not have grounding evidence. The audit must distinguish this failure mode from general accuracy issues and from biased outputs.

Which auditing focus addresses the requirement?

choices.text: Audit for hallucinations by sampling responses and verifying that asserted facts are supported by retrieved sources or known ground truth.
choices.explanation: Hallucination auditing is the targeted check for ungrounded fabricated content.

choices.text: Audit only access logs to verify who used the assistant during the period.
choices.explanation: Access auditing does not measure factual correctness.

choices.text: Audit for bias and fairness across demographic subgroups.
choices.explanation: Bias auditing is a different failure mode and not the requested focus.

choices.text: Audit response confidence levels only.
choices.explanation: Confidence does not by itself indicate whether the content is grounded or fabricated.

questions.tip: Match the audit to the specific failure mode being investigated.
questions.explanation:
Hallucination auditing specifically targets ungrounded fabricated assertions.

**Why it works:** Comparing model claims to retrieved evidence or ground truth identifies fabrication, which is distinct from accuracy or bias.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Access only: wrong question.
- Bias and fairness: different failure mode.
- Confidence only: not a fabrication signal.

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, implement monitoring and auditing for AI systems.
questions.question:
Security operations is tuning detection on the AI gateway. The team wants to alert when a single client suddenly issues many prompts in a short window or when the global request rate spikes outside business norms, both of which could indicate abuse or a model denial-of-service attempt. They also want to see the baseline trend over time.

Which monitoring control should the team configure?

choices.text: Configure rate monitoring on the gateway with per-client and global request thresholds, baseline trending, and alerts on anomalies.
choices.explanation: Rate monitoring with per-client and global views directly addresses the requirement.

choices.text: Alert only when monthly cost crosses a fixed budget.
choices.explanation: Cost-only alerts trigger after damage is done and miss short bursts.

choices.text: Forward GPU utilization metrics from inference nodes to the dashboard.
choices.explanation: GPU utilization does not show per-client request behavior.

choices.text: Disable all gateway metrics to reduce overhead.
choices.explanation: Disabling metrics removes the signal the team needs.

questions.tip: Pick the metric that measures request volume directly, both per client and globally.
questions.explanation:
Rate monitoring is the targeted control for abuse and denial-of-service patterns.

**Why it works:** Per-client and global request rates with baselines surface both targeted abuse and global spikes.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Monthly cost alerts: too coarse.
- GPU utilization: indirect.
- Disable metrics: defeats the purpose.

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, implement monitoring and auditing for AI systems.
questions.question:
The platform team is establishing baseline monitoring and auditing for a new generative AI service. Requirements include keeping prompt and response logs tamper resistant, ensuring the logs themselves do not become a target for data exfiltration, and providing assurance that the service is treating different user demographics consistently. The team needs to pick two foundational controls that address these aims.

Which TWO controls should the team implement?

choices.text: Apply log protection by writing logs to an append-only store with strict access controls and integrity checks.
choices.explanation: Log protection addresses tamper resistance and limits exfiltration risk.

choices.text: Schedule periodic bias and fairness audits comparing outputs across demographic subgroups.
choices.explanation: Bias and fairness audits address consistent treatment across user demographics.

choices.text: Increase the model's maximum response length to provide more context.
choices.explanation: Longer responses do not contribute to log protection or fairness assurance.

choices.text: Disable inference logging during high-traffic periods to reduce storage cost.
choices.explanation: Disabling logging removes the audit trail the requirements depend on.

choices.text: Replace the gateway with a direct connection from clients to the model provider.
choices.explanation: Bypassing the gateway removes the inspection point needed for both monitoring and auditing.

questions.tip: Pair an integrity control on the logs with an outcome audit on the model.
questions.explanation:
Append-only protected logs and recurring bias and fairness audits address both the integrity and the fairness requirements.

**Why it works:** Log protection secures the audit trail; fairness audits provide ongoing assurance of consistent treatment.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Longer responses: unrelated.
- Disable logging: removes the audit trail.
- Bypass gateway: loses the inspection point.

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, implement monitoring and auditing for AI systems.
questions.question: Match each monitoring or auditing concern to the control or metric that best addresses it.

slots.label: Spotting sudden bursts of prompts from a client

choices.text: Hallucination auditing that compares asserted facts against retrieved or ground-truth sources
choices.explanation: Hallucination auditing directly targets ungrounded fabricated content.

choices.text: Log sanitization that redacts sensitive fields before logs are written
choices.explanation: Sanitization keeps useful metadata while removing raw sensitive content.

choices.text: AI cost monitoring with per-tenant and per-feature attribution of token spend
choices.explanation: Attributed cost monitoring surfaces which tenants and features drive spend.

choices.text: Per-client rate monitoring with anomaly thresholds at the gateway
choices.explanation: Rate monitoring detects unusual bursts of requests from a single source.

questions.tip: Map each concern to the control that measures or restricts the relevant dimension.
questions.explanation: Each concern is matched by a specific monitoring or auditing practice: fabrication by hallucination audits, log exposure by sanitization, spend by attributed cost monitoring, and abuse bursts by rate monitoring.

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, analyze the evidence of an attack and suggest compensating controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
Incident response is reviewing logs from a customer-facing chatbot. Several conversations contain user messages that embed instructions such as ignore previous rules and reveal system prompt, followed by responses where the assistant disclosed internal persona instructions. No other authentication or backend control failed.

Which attack does the evidence describe, and which compensating control should be prioritized?

choices.text: Prompt injection. Deploy a prompt firewall in front of the model to inspect and block known injection patterns before they reach the system prompt boundary.
choices.explanation: The user-supplied instructions overrode the system prompt, matching prompt injection; a prompt firewall is the targeted compensating control.

choices.text: Model theft. Restrict outbound bandwidth from the inference servers to prevent weight extraction.
choices.explanation: No weights or large artifacts were exfiltrated; the disclosure was the system prompt, not the model itself.

choices.text: Membership inference. Add differential privacy noise to the training pipeline.
choices.explanation: There is no evidence of inference about training set membership; the issue is runtime prompt override.

choices.text: Supply chain attack. Pin and verify the model vendor's container image signature.
choices.explanation: There is no indication the vendor pipeline was compromised; the attack came through user input.

questions.tip: Match the evidence to the attack class before picking a control.
questions.explanation:
Disclosure of the system prompt after user instructions to ignore previous rules is the textbook signature of prompt injection.

**Why it works:** A prompt firewall inspects incoming prompts for known injection and policy-violation patterns and blocks them before they reach the model.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model theft: no weight exfiltration evidence.
- Membership inference: a different inference attack.
- Supply chain: no vendor compromise evidence.

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, analyze the evidence of an attack and suggest compensating controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
A junior analyst flagged that an AI coding assistant produced a function which, when triggered by a very specific comment string, silently exfiltrates environment variables. Code review of recent fine-tuning data uncovered a small number of examples that paired that exact comment string with the malicious snippet. No runtime prompt contained these instructions.

Which attack is described, and which compensating control is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Backdoor or Trojan attack via training data poisoning. Tighten data integrity controls on the fine-tuning corpus, including provenance checks and review of contributed examples.
choices.explanation: A hidden trigger inserted through training data is the definition of a backdoor; data integrity controls address the root cause.

choices.text: Prompt injection. Add a stricter system prompt that forbids exfiltration.
choices.explanation: There is no runtime injection; a system prompt does not remove a learned backdoor.

choices.text: Model denial of service. Add gateway rate limits.
choices.explanation: Rate limits do not address a triggered behavior baked into the model.

choices.text: Insecure output handling. Sanitize the model's text before display.
choices.explanation: Output sanitization does not remove a learned malicious behavior; it only filters the result.

questions.tip: If the malicious behavior is tied to a specific learned trigger, look at the training data.
questions.explanation:
A specific trigger paired with a malicious payload in the fine-tuning corpus indicates a backdoor introduced via data poisoning.

**Why it works:** Strengthening data integrity, provenance, and contributor review prevents poisoned examples from reaching training.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Prompt injection: runtime mechanism, not the cause here.
- Rate limits: unrelated to backdoors.
- Output sanitization: does not remove the underlying behavior.

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, analyze the evidence of an attack and suggest compensating controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
Monitoring shows that a single API key has issued millions of nearly identical inference requests over several hours, with carefully varied inputs designed to probe the model's decision boundary. Researchers suspect the attacker is trying to build a functional copy of the model from the input and output pairs.

Which attack does this match, and what compensating control should be applied first?

choices.text: Model theft via query extraction. Apply aggressive rate limiting and per-key query quotas at the gateway and revoke abusive keys.
choices.explanation: High-volume probing for extraction is model theft; rate limiting and quotas constrain the exposure.

choices.text: Prompt injection. Add a prompt firewall to filter the input strings.
choices.explanation: The inputs are not crafted to hijack the system prompt; they are crafted to probe the model.

choices.text: Data poisoning. Quarantine the training pipeline.
choices.explanation: Inference probing does not modify training data.

choices.text: Insecure plug-in design. Disable all model plug-ins.
choices.explanation: There is no plug-in involved in the described behavior.

questions.tip: Match the volume and intent of the queries to the attack class.
questions.explanation:
High-volume boundary probing on inference is the standard pattern for model theft via extraction.

**Why it works:** Per-key rate limits and quotas reduce the volume of input-output pairs an attacker can collect, raising the cost of extraction.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Prompt injection: wrong mechanism.
- Data poisoning: targets training, not inference.
- Plug-in design: not implicated.

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, analyze the evidence of an attack and suggest compensating controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
An autonomous AI assistant with tools for email, calendar, and finance approvals received a meeting note containing hidden instructions to wire funds to an external account. The agent attempted the transfer without asking the user. Review confirmed the assistant had standing approval rights on the finance tool.

Which combination of attack and compensating control fits the evidence?

choices.text: Excessive agency exploited via indirect prompt injection. Apply least privilege to the agent's tool scopes and require human confirmation for sensitive actions such as transfers.
choices.explanation: Standing approval rights are excessive agency; the injection rode in through retrieved content.

choices.text: Model inversion. Encrypt the training data at rest.
choices.explanation: There is no attempt to infer training data from outputs; this is an agency abuse.

choices.text: Insecure output handling. HTML-encode the agent's responses before display.
choices.explanation: Encoding the response does not stop the agent from taking the action.

choices.text: Model denial of service. Add token caps to the agent's prompts.
choices.explanation: There is no resource exhaustion attack here.

questions.tip: Standing approvals plus an injection trigger point to excessive agency.
questions.explanation:
The standing finance approval gave the agent more autonomy than the task required, allowing a single injection to cause real-world harm.

**Why it works:** Reducing the agent's permissions to least privilege and gating sensitive actions on user confirmation directly compensates for the excessive agency.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model inversion: different attack class.
- Output handling: does not prevent the action.
- DoS: not the pattern.

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, analyze the evidence of an attack and suggest compensating controls for AI systems.
questions.question:
Forensics has confirmed that an attacker successfully jailbroke a public chatbot by chaining a long roleplay prompt with hidden control characters, then used the assistant to generate disallowed content. Repeat attempts from different IP ranges followed within hours. Leadership wants compensating controls that reduce the success rate of future jailbreaks and limit the blast radius of any single abusive client.

Which TWO compensating controls should the team implement?

choices.text: Deploy a prompt firewall with updated jailbreak detection rules and continuous adversarial regression testing against the guardrails.
choices.explanation: This raises the bar against the same and similar jailbreak chains.

choices.text: Enforce per-client rate limiting on the gateway so a single abusive caller cannot drive sustained attempts.
choices.explanation: Rate limiting contains the blast radius of any single abusive client.

choices.text: Disable TLS to reduce overhead during high-traffic periods.
choices.explanation: Disabling transport security is harmful and unrelated to jailbreak mitigation.

choices.text: Grant the chatbot agent broader tool permissions to reduce user friction.
choices.explanation: Broader permissions increase, not reduce, blast radius.

choices.text: Remove the system prompt entirely so the model has no instructions to override.
choices.explanation: Removing the system prompt eliminates the policy the firewall and model are meant to enforce.

questions.tip: Combine a control that raises attack cost with one that limits per-client impact.
questions.explanation:
Updated guardrail rules with regression testing handle the jailbreak technique; per-client rate limiting handles the volume and repeat-offender pattern.

**Why it works:** Together they reduce success likelihood per attempt and the rate at which any one attacker can try.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disable TLS: harmful and irrelevant.
- Broader agent permissions: amplifies impact.
- No system prompt: removes the policy baseline.

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, analyze the evidence of an attack and suggest compensating controls for AI systems.
questions.question: Match each observed attack pattern to the compensating control that most directly addresses it.

slots.label: Standing tool approvals abused after an indirect prompt injection
High-volume probing of a public inference API to reconstruct the model
Hidden trigger in fine-tuning data causing malicious behavior on demand
Runtime user instructions overriding the system prompt

choices.text: Apply least privilege to agent tools and require user confirmation for sensitive actions
choices.explanation: Reducing standing capability addresses excessive agency exposed by injection.

choices.text: Enforce per-key rate limits and query quotas on the inference gateway
choices.explanation: Rate and quota controls raise the cost of extraction attempts.

choices.text: Strengthen data integrity controls and provenance review on the training corpus
choices.explanation: Training data integrity removes the root cause of backdoors.

choices.text: Deploy a prompt firewall to inspect and block injection and jailbreak patterns
choices.explanation: A prompt firewall sits between user input and model to enforce policy at the prompt boundary.

questions.tip: Match each attack class to the control layer that addresses its mechanism.
questions.explanation: Each attack pattern has a layer it exploits: agent capability, inference volume, training pipeline, or runtime prompt. The compensating control belongs at the same layer.

skills: 3.1: Given a scenario, use AI-enabled tools to facilitate security tasks.
questions.question:
During a code review sprint, a development team wants real-time AI assistance that highlights insecure functions, suggests safer alternatives, and flags hardcoded secrets as engineers type. The lead requires the assistance to surface inside the editor without copying code into an external chat window, and to respect the existing repository configuration.

Which AI-enabled tool category best fits this requirement?

choices.text: IDE plug-in that integrates a code-aware AI assistant directly into the editor workspace.
choices.explanation: IDE plug-ins surface AI suggestions inline as the developer works, without forcing manual context-sharing.

choices.text: Standalone chatbot accessed through a public web portal for ad-hoc code questions.
choices.explanation: A public chatbot requires copying snippets out of the IDE, breaking the inline workflow the lead requires.

choices.text: Browser plug-in that watches page DOM events for suspicious form inputs.
choices.explanation: Browser plug-ins target web pages, not source code under active development in an IDE.

choices.text: CLI plug-in that scans compiled artifacts after a release build completes.
choices.explanation: Post-build CLI scanning runs too late to give real-time feedback while engineers type.

questions.tip: Match the delivery surface of the AI tool to where the work is actually happening.
questions.explanation:
An IDE plug-in places the AI assistant in the same context as the code, allowing immediate, in-line suggestions without leaving the development environment.

**Why it works:** The plug-in reads the active buffer and project context, so secrets, insecure APIs, and risky patterns can be highlighted as the code is written.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public chatbot: forces manual copy-paste outside the IDE
- Browser plug-in: scoped to web pages, not source
- CLI build scanner: runs after the fact, not in real time

skills: 3.1: Given a scenario, use AI-enabled tools to facilitate security tasks.
questions.question:
The SOC lead wants a single AI assistant that can pull live ticket data from the case management system, query the SIEM for related events, and read enrichment from the threat intelligence platform, all through one standardized interface. The architecture must let each backend expose only the tools and resources the assistant is permitted to call.

Which approach satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Deploy a Model Context Protocol server in front of each backend so the assistant calls a uniform tool interface.
choices.explanation: MCP servers expose tools and resources through a standard schema, letting one assistant connect to many systems with scoped permissions.

choices.text: Embed long-lived API keys for every backend directly into the assistant's system prompt.
choices.explanation: Hard-coded keys in prompts leak credentials and offer no per-tool authorization control.

choices.text: Configure the assistant to scrape each backend's web UI through a headless browser session.
choices.explanation: Screen scraping is brittle, unauthenticated by design, and cannot expose a controlled tool surface.

choices.text: Train a single large model on a static export of the ticketing, SIEM, and TI data each morning.
choices.explanation: Static training data is stale and cannot answer live questions about current cases.

questions.tip: Look for a standardized integration layer rather than per-system bespoke wiring.
questions.explanation:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines a server interface that exposes tools, resources, and prompts to a client model in a controlled, scoped way.

**Why it works:** Each backend implements an MCP server that advertises only the actions and data the assistant is allowed to use, giving consistent integration and authorization.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Hard-coded keys in prompts: insecure and not granular
- Headless browser scraping: brittle and unauthorized
- Static daily training: cannot reflect live ticket and event state

skills: 3.1: Given a scenario, use AI-enabled tools to facilitate security tasks.
questions.question:
Following a noisy week of EDR alerts, an analyst wants the on-call assistant to read each new detection, pull the affected host inventory, and produce a short, prioritized briefing for the morning standup. The expectation is a paragraph per incident with key indicators and the suggested next action, drawn from raw alert text and runbook excerpts.

Which AI use case best describes this workload?

choices.text: Summarization of alert and runbook text into concise human-readable briefings.
choices.explanation: Reducing long alert and runbook content into prioritized paragraphs is a classic summarization task.

choices.text: Signature matching against a static set of malware hashes.
choices.explanation: Signature matching produces verdicts, not narrative briefings.

choices.text: Translation of alert text into a target natural language.
choices.explanation: Translation changes the language, not the length or structure of the content.

choices.text: Fraud detection based on transactional anomaly scoring.
choices.explanation: Fraud detection is unrelated to EDR alert summarization.

questions.tip: Identify the transformation being applied to the input text.
questions.explanation:
Summarization condenses longer source material into a shorter form while preserving key facts and next steps.

**Why it works:** The assistant is being asked to reduce alert detail and runbook text into a briefing paragraph per incident.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Signature matching: yields verdicts, not narratives
- Translation: language conversion, not condensation
- Fraud detection: a different problem domain entirely

skills: 3.1: Given a scenario, use AI-enabled tools to facilitate security tasks.
questions.question:
The application security architect is drafting a data-flow diagram for a new payments microservice and wants an AI assistant to help enumerate STRIDE categories, suggest trust boundaries, and propose mitigations for each component as the diagram evolves. The goal is to produce a structured artefact that engineering and risk can both review.

Which AI security use case is the assistant primarily supporting?

choices.text: Threat modeling, by structuring components and abuse cases into a reviewable artefact.
choices.explanation: Enumerating STRIDE categories and trust boundaries against a data-flow diagram is the core of threat modeling.

choices.text: Automated penetration testing, by running exploits against the live service.
choices.explanation: No live target is being exercised; this is a design-time analysis.

choices.text: Anomaly detection, by baselining transaction rates against historical norms.
choices.explanation: Anomaly detection works on runtime telemetry, not architecture diagrams.

choices.text: Code linting, by enforcing style rules across the microservice source tree.
choices.explanation: Linting targets source code style and quality, not architectural trust boundaries.

questions.tip: Look for the phase of the development lifecycle the activity belongs to.
questions.explanation:
Threat modeling is performed at design time and uses structured frameworks like STRIDE to reason about components, data flows, and trust boundaries.

**Why it works:** The assistant is helping reason about abuse cases and mitigations on a diagram, not running code or scanning telemetry.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Automated pentesting: requires a live target
- Anomaly detection: runtime data driven
- Code linting: focused on code style, not design

skills: 3.1: Given a scenario, use AI-enabled tools to facilitate security tasks.

A managed service provider is rolling out AI-assisted workflows for its analysts. Leadership wants two clear, measurable security use cases where AI tooling reliably reduces analyst time on high-volume, pattern-heavy work without replacing human judgment on novel incidents.

choices.text: Anomaly detection across authentication logs to surface deviations from established baselines.
choices.explanation: Statistical pattern work over high-volume telemetry is well suited to AI assistance.

choices.text: Summarization of long incident timelines into briefings for handover between shifts.
choices.explanation: Reducing long texts into structured briefings is a high-volume, low-judgment task AI handles well.

AI tooling shines in high-volume, pattern-rich tasks where outputs can be reviewed by an analyst before action.

- Regulator disclosure: a legal judgment call
- Emergency change approval: a human accountability decision
